prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, in which neutral atoms held at a magic wavelength allow frequency measurements at the 1e-18 level.

statement.case_for: I keep B041 as my single-part position. The scientific case is unchanged by the first round, and nobody has disputed its maturity: a concrete idea (the magic wavelength that cancels the light shift while the atoms are held tightly enough to remove Doppler and recoil shifts), an early demonstration, and then reproduction by competing groups in Sr, Yb and Hg with agreeing numbers, checked by fibre-link comparisons between laboratories. That is the experimental pattern I trust. The new capability is physical and checkable: gravitational redshift resolved over millimetres, tighter limits on drifts of constants, and a primary-standard route to the redefinition of the second. The two-name credit is also the cleanest on the shortlist, because the proposal (Katori) and the performance frontier (Ye) are both covered without leaving a gap. In answer to the chair's question, I would word the citation around invention and realization of the lattice clock, so that the lattice concept is the discovery and the accuracy figure is only the evidence that it works. I will not lean on null results for constants or dark matter in the citation.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection remains novelty relative to the 2005 prize (combs) and the 2012 prize (single-ion control and clocks): a committee can read lattice clocks as a very successful second-generation advance in frequency metrology. My answer, that a neutral-atom ensemble at a magic wavelength is a different principle from a single trapped ion and that the comb is the ruler and not the clock, is an argument and not a proof, and members outside atomic physics may reasonably weigh it differently. The fundamental-physics output so far is constraints, the redefinition of the second has not yet happened, and priority between Katori, Ye and the PTB, SYRTE, NIST and RIKEN groups is recalled from memory. B018 has far broader support (six of eight), a conventional theory-to-experiment arc, and a trio that all its supporters state identically; if its attribution problem were small I would have no principled basis to put B041 ahead of it.

responses.point: Mehlig moved to B018 but notes that topological band theory belongs to a lineage already recognised in 2016, so a committee could judge it a refinement, and that the attribution gap (BHZ, Zhang, the 3D work) is real.
responses.response: I think your 2016 objection is the more serious of the two for B018, and I am glad it is on the table, because it is the same kind of novelty question that is being put to my own candidate and we should apply it evenly. The 2016 prize covered topological invariants in integer quantum Hall and Haldane-type phases and topological defect transitions. Time-reversal-invariant Z2 insulators without a magnetic field are, to my understanding, a distinct class with a distinct experiment, so I would not call B018 merely a refinement; but I defer to the condensed-matter members on that. My own reservation about B018 stays on attribution. If Molenkamp's HgTe experiment was a realization of the BHZ proposal, then the experimentalist and the guiding proposal come from different people, and a citation naming Kane, Mele and Molenkamp has to say that clearly. On the pattern of reasoning, I would ask that the committee apply to both candidates the same test of 'is this a new principle or an improvement of one already rewarded'.

responses.point: The chair raised a two-part prize pairing B018 with a precision-measurement achievement such as B041, and asked how the three-laureate limit could be honoured for both parts.
responses.response: I considered this seriously, because it would let the committee honour both camps. The arithmetic does not work without damaging one part: B018 with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp already uses three people, and adding Katori and Ye would make five. Cutting B018 to two names would drop either the theory or the experiment, which is the exact attribution gap its supporters want to avoid, and cutting B041 to one name would separate the proposal from the demonstration. I would rather present one prize with an honest, complete credit than two prizes with a visible compromise in each. So I do not propose a pairing, and I would not want a two-part configuration to be reached only to resolve the support count, which several of us have said is not a measure of merit.

responses.point: Olsson asks whether the Molenkamp HgTe experiment was guided by the BHZ proposal, so that the credit for Kane, Mele and Molenkamp would honour the 2005 concept and a 2007 experiment that followed a different proposal, and says this should be checked against the primary papers.
responses.response: I agree that this is the open question for B018 and that it can be settled by reading the papers instead of arguing from memory. As I recall, BHZ appeared in 2006 and the HgTe measurement in 2007, and the paper itself cites the proposal, so the guiding role seems documented, but I have not verified it and the committee should ask the experts to check. If the answer is that BHZ was the decisive step, I would say the committee faces a harder attribution choice than the shortlist suggests. I accept the same standard for my candidate: I have asked Eva Lindroth, and I ask again now, to check the magic-wavelength and first lattice-clock dates, since the Katori-versus-Ye split rests on them.

responses.point: Eriksson calls B018 a verified discovery with nearly two decades of independent confirmation, arguably overdue, and notes that condensed-matter members may favour it more than they can judge against atomic-physics candidates.
responses.response: I appreciate the candour in your last point, and I would add the same caution about my own side: atomic and metrology members are likely to rate B041 more favourably than the condensed-matter members can check, so neither camp should treat its own enthusiasm as committee-wide merit. On substance I accept your point on maturity and I do not call B018 premature. Where we differ is how much the attribution gap weighs against it. You and the others treat it as a wording matter and I treat it as a scientific question about who made the decisive step. I have moved a little on this since round 1, since six colleagues state the trio identically and none sees a different trio, but I have not moved my preferred configuration.

responses.point: Lindroth shares the B041 configuration and the same two-name credit and asks whether the lattice clock is distinct enough from the 2005 and 2012 prizes; she also defers to condensed-matter colleagues on B018.
responses.response: We agree on the science, and I want to add a point of disagreement on what would move us. The chair asked what evidence would move the B041 supporters. For me it would be a primary-paper check showing that the B018 attribution is clean (BHZ not decisive for HgTe) and that Katori's priority is weaker than I recall; either one would make me put B018 first. On the other side, a decision by the committee that the lattice clock is only a refinement of the 2005 and 2012 ideas would also weaken B041. I would not give up the citation wording just to improve the count, and I would prefer that we both say plainly that our B041 case is a case about a new measurement capability, not a new phase of matter.

uncertainties: Whether lattice clocks count as a distinct achievement from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-clock prizes, or as a successor improvement; the same test should be applied to B018 against 2016.
Priority and decisiveness of Katori versus Ye and the PTB, SYRTE, NIST/JILA and RIKEN groups, recalled from memory and unverified.
Whether a prize on measurement method should wait for the redefinition of the second.
Whether the BHZ proposal was decisive for the HgTe experiment, which would decide how much the B018 attribution gap weighs against it; a primary-paper check would answer this.
How much of the committee's support for B018 reflects condensed-matter members' own field preference, and how much of my support for B041 reflects mine.
statement.conflict_note: No tie to Katori, Ye or their groups, and no collaboration. For disclosure: my group works on laser stabilization using slow light in spectral-hole-burning crystals, a neighbouring technique to clock-laser technology but not shared work with the candidates. I also have institutional links to WACQT/Chalmers and the quantum-memory community, which would call for recusal or caution on B020 and on quantum-information candidates; none is in my preferred configuration or in my alternatives. No change from round 1.
